element.name: Qualification Management
element.documentation:
Definition: Qualification Management enables the electronic validation and verification of the qualifications (any information linked to an individual with respect to the education and employment status) of the professionals against specific requirements defined by relevant legislations.
Source: Oracle
Source reference: https://www.oracle.com/a/ocom/docs/applications/erp/oracle-supplier-qualification-management-cloud-ds.pdf
Additional information: The Qualification Management Digital Business Capability (QMDBC) is a comprehensive framework and set of digital tools designed to facilitate and enhance the interoperability of IT systems and processes related to qualifications management among member states and private companies in Europe. It aims to streamline and harmonize the exchange of qualification-related information, ensuring consistency, efficiency, and transparency across borders.
At its core, the QMDBC encompasses a range of digital solutions and standards that enable the seamless sharing, recognition, and validation of qualifications across different countries and organizations. It provides a common platform for member states and private companies to collaborate and exchange information on qualifications, enabling individuals to have their qualifications recognized and valued in various contexts.
One of the key components of the QMDBC is a centralized database or repository that stores and manages qualification-related data. This database serves as a single source of truth, containing information on qualifications, competencies, skills, and other relevant attributes. It allows member states and private companies to access and verify qualifications, ensuring accuracy and reliability in the recognition process.
The QMDBC also incorporates standardized data formats and protocols to ensure compatibility and interoperability among different IT systems. This includes the use of common data models, metadata standards, and communication protocols, enabling seamless integration and exchange of qualification data between member states and private companies. These standards facilitate the automated processing and validation of qualifications, reducing administrative burdens and improving the efficiency of recognition procedures.
Furthermore, the QMDBC includes digital tools and services that support the management and assessment of qualifications. These tools enable member states and private companies to evaluate and compare qualifications, assess their relevance and equivalence, and make informed decisions regarding recognition and validation. They may include online assessment platforms, qualification frameworks, competency mapping tools, and other digital resources that enhance the transparency and objectivity of the qualification recognition process.
In addition to the technical aspects, the QMDBC also encompasses governance and policy frameworks that guide the implementation and operation of the interoperability infrastructure. This includes the establishment of common rules, procedures, and quality assurance mechanisms to ensure the reliability and trustworthiness of qualification information. It also involves the collaboration and coordination among member states, private companies, and relevant stakeholders to address legal, regulatory, and ethical considerations associated with qualification recognition and interoperability.
Overall, the Qualification Management Digital Business Capability plays a crucial role in promoting the harmonization and interoperability of qualification management systems across Europe. By providing a standardized and efficient framework for exchanging qualification-related information, it facilitates the recognition and validation of qualifications, enhances labor mobility, and supports the development of a skilled and competitive workforce in the European Union.
Example: The Qualification Management Digital Business Capability can be applied in various ways to enhance European IT interoperability among member states and private companies. Here are a few examples:
1. Digital Credentialing: The capability can be used to establish a standardized system for issuing and managing digital credentials, such as diplomas, certifications, and licenses. This would enable seamless recognition of qualifications across member states and private companies, reducing administrative burden and facilitating mobility of IT professionals.
2. Cross-border Recognition: The capability can support the development of a common framework for recognizing qualifications across European countries. By digitizing and harmonizing qualification management processes, member states and private companies can easily verify and accept qualifications obtained in other jurisdictions, promoting workforce mobility and facilitating cross-border collaborations.
3. Competency Mapping: The capability can enable the creation of a comprehensive competency mapping system, which aligns IT qualifications with specific job roles and skills required in the industry. This would help member states and private companies in identifying and matching the right talent for specific IT projects or job vacancies, ensuring a better fit between qualifications and job requirements.
4. Interoperable Learning Management Systems: The capability can facilitate the integration of different learning management systems used by member states and private companies. This would enable seamless exchange of training and educational resources, fostering collaboration and knowledge sharing among European IT stakeholders.
5. Quality Assurance and Accreditation: The capability can support the establishment of a unified quality assurance and accreditation framework for IT qualifications. By digitizing and automating the accreditation processes, member states and private companies can ensure consistent quality standards across Europe, enhancing trust and reliability in the IT workforce.
Overall, the Qualification Management Digital Business Capability can play a crucial role in promoting harmonization, standardization, and interoperability of IT qualifications among member states and private companies in Europe.

element.name: Data Governance
element.documentation:
Description: The Data Governance Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of an organization to effectively manage and govern its data assets. It involves establishing policies, procedures, and frameworks to ensure data quality, integrity, security, and compliance. This capability enables organizations to have a holistic view of their data, make informed decisions based on reliable information, and ensure that data is used in a consistent and controlled manner across the enterprise. It also involves implementing data governance processes and tools to monitor and enforce data standards, resolve data-related issues, and enable data-driven decision-making at all levels of the organization.
Additional information: The Data Governance Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of an organization to effectively manage and govern its data assets in a digital business environment. It encompasses the policies, processes, and practices that ensure the availability, integrity, confidentiality, and usability of data across the enterprise.
Data governance involves establishing a framework that defines the roles, responsibilities, and decision-making processes related to data management. It aims to ensure that data is accurate, consistent, and reliable, and that it complies with relevant regulations and standards. The digital aspect of data governance emphasizes the need to manage data in the context of digital transformation initiatives and the increasing reliance on digital technologies.
Key components of the Data Governance Digital Business Capability include:
1. Data Strategy: Developing a strategic plan that aligns data governance objectives with the overall business strategy. This involves defining the vision, goals, and objectives for data governance and identifying the key initiatives required to achieve them.
2. Data Policies and Standards: Establishing policies and standards that govern the collection, storage, processing, and sharing of data. These policies define data quality requirements, data classification and handling guidelines, data retention and disposal policies, and data privacy and security measures.
3. Data Stewardship: Assigning data stewards who are responsible for ensuring the quality, integrity, and compliance of data within their respective domains. Data stewards collaborate with data owners, users, and IT teams to define and enforce data standards, resolve data-related issues, and promote data governance best practices.
4. Data Quality Management: Implementing processes and tools to monitor, measure, and improve the quality of data. This includes data profiling, data cleansing, data validation, and data enrichment activities to ensure that data is accurate, complete, and consistent.
5. Data Privacy and Security: Establishing controls and measures to protect sensitive data from unauthorized access, disclosure, or misuse. This involves implementing data encryption, access controls, data masking, and data anonymization techniques to safeguard data privacy and comply with data protection regulations.
6. Data Lifecycle Management: Defining processes and procedures to manage the entire lifecycle of data, from creation to archival or disposal. This includes data capture, storage, integration, transformation, and archival strategies, as well as data backup and recovery mechanisms.
7. Data Governance Organization: Establishing a dedicated data governance team or committee responsible for overseeing and coordinating data governance activities. This team ensures that data governance policies and practices are effectively implemented, and it provides guidance and support to data stewards and other stakeholders.
8. Data Governance Tools and Technologies: Implementing data governance tools and technologies that facilitate data management, data quality monitoring, metadata management, and data lineage tracking. These tools enable automation, collaboration, and reporting capabilities to support efficient and effective data governance practices.
By developing and maturing the Data Governance Digital Business Capability, organizations can ensure that their data assets are effectively managed, protected, and leveraged to drive business value, support decision-making processes, and enable digital transformation initiatives.
Example: The Data Governance Digital Business Capability in the public sector refers to the ability to establish and enforce policies, procedures, and standards for managing data assets effectively. Here are some real examples of this capability in action:

The Data Governance Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of an organization to effectively manage and govern its data assets in a digital business environment. It encompasses the policies, processes, and practices that ensure the availability, integrity, confidentiality, and usability of data across the enterprise.
Data governance involves establishing a framework that defines the roles, responsibilities, and decision-making processes related to data management. It aims to ensure that data is accurate, consistent, and reliable, and that it complies with relevant regulations and standards. The digital aspect of data governance emphasizes the need to manage data in the context of digital transformation initiatives and the increasing reliance on digital technologies.
Key components of the Data Governance Digital Business Capability include:
1. Data Strategy: Developing a strategic plan that aligns data governance objectives with the overall business strategy. This involves defining the vision, goals, and objectives for data governance and identifying the key initiatives required to achieve them.
2. Data Policies and Standards: Establishing policies and standards that govern the collection, storage, processing, and sharing of data. These policies define data quality requirements, data classification and handling guidelines, data retention and disposal policies, and data privacy and security measures.
3. Data Stewardship: Assigning data stewards who are responsible for ensuring the quality, integrity, and compliance of data within their respective domains. Data stewards collaborate with data owners, users, and IT teams to define and enforce data standards, resolve data-related issues, and promote data governance best practices.
4. Data Quality Management: Implementing processes and tools to monitor, measure, and improve the quality of data. This includes data profiling, data cleansing, data validation, and data enrichment activities to ensure that data is accurate, complete, and consistent.
5. Data Privacy and Security: Establishing controls and measures to protect sensitive data from unauthorized access, disclosure, or misuse. This involves implementing data encryption, access controls, data masking, and data anonymization techniques to safeguard data privacy and comply with data protection regulations.
6. Data Lifecycle Management: Defining processes and procedures to manage the entire lifecycle of data, from creation to archival or disposal. This includes data capture, storage, integration, transformation, and archival strategies, as well as data backup and recovery mechanisms.
7. Data Governance Organization: Establishing a dedicated data governance team or committee responsible for overseeing and coordinating data governance activities. This team ensures that data governance policies and practices are effectively implemented, and it provides guidance and support to data stewards and other stakeholders.
8. Data Governance Tools and Technologies: Implementing data governance tools and technologies that facilitate data management, data quality monitoring, metadata management, and data lineage tracking. These tools enable automation, collaboration, and reporting capabilities to support efficient and effective data governance practices.
By developing and maturing the Data Governance Digital Business Capability, organizations can ensure that their data assets are effectively managed, protected, and leveraged to drive business value, support decision-making processes, and enable digital transformation initiatives.

element.name: Digital Twin
element.documentation:
Definition: Digital Twin enables the creation of a digital copy of reality, that allows to simulate and find answers in a risk free and secure environment. The coupling of the physical and digital world enables to monitor both systems, prevent issues, develop new opportunities and simulate future outcomes. It is based on three main pillars: Connectivity, Digitalization, Intelligence.
Source: Michael Grieves
Source reference: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334599683_Virtually_Intelligent_Product_Systems_Digital_and_Physical_Twins
Additional information: The Digital Twin Digital Business Capability (DT-DBC) is a concept that aims to enhance IT interoperability among member states and private companies within the European Union (EU). It is a strategic initiative that leverages digital technologies to create virtual replicas or representations of physical entities, such as products, systems, or processes.
The primary objective of the DT-DBC is to enable seamless data exchange, collaboration, and integration across various domains, sectors, and organizations. It seeks to establish a standardized framework and infrastructure that allows member states and private companies to share and utilize digital twins effectively.
Digital twins are dynamic, real-time digital models that mirror the physical entities they represent. They are equipped with sensors, data analytics capabilities, and connectivity, enabling them to capture and transmit data about their physical counterparts. This data can include information about the entity's performance, behavior, condition, and environment.
The DT-DBC aims to facilitate the creation, management, and utilization of digital twins across the EU by establishing common standards, protocols, and interfaces. It promotes the adoption of open and interoperable technologies, ensuring that digital twins can seamlessly interact and exchange data regardless of their origin or location.
By implementing the DT-DBC, member states and private companies can achieve several benefits. Firstly, it enables improved decision-making by providing real-time insights into the performance and behavior of physical entities. This allows for proactive maintenance, optimization, and predictive analysis, leading to increased efficiency, reduced costs, and enhanced reliability.
Secondly, the DT-DBC fosters collaboration and knowledge sharing among stakeholders. It enables different organizations to work together on common projects, share data, and leverage each other's expertise. This promotes innovation, accelerates development cycles, and facilitates the creation of new products, services, and business models.
Furthermore, the DT-DBC contributes to the digital transformation of industries and sectors. It enables the integration of digital twins into existing IT systems, processes, and workflows, creating a seamless and connected ecosystem. This integration can span across domains such as manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, energy, and more, enabling cross-sector collaboration and innovation.
To ensure the successful implementation of the DT-DBC, several challenges need to be addressed. These include data privacy and security concerns, standardization of data formats and interfaces, harmonization of regulations and policies, and the development of robust infrastructure and connectivity.
In conclusion, the Digital Twin Digital Business Capability is a strategic initiative aimed at enhancing IT interoperability among member states and private companies within the European Union. By leveraging digital twins, it enables seamless data exchange, collaboration, and integration, leading to improved decision-making, increased efficiency, and accelerated innovation.
Example: The application of Digital Twin Digital Business Capability can greatly benefit European IT interoperability among member states and private companies. Here are a few examples:
1. Cross-border data sharing: Digital Twin technology can facilitate seamless data sharing and interoperability between different member states and private companies. It allows for the creation of virtual replicas of physical assets or systems, enabling real-time data exchange and collaboration across borders. This can be particularly useful in areas such as transportation, energy, and healthcare, where cross-border data sharing is crucial for efficient operations.
2. Standardization and harmonization: Digital Twin technology can help in standardizing and harmonizing IT systems and processes across member states and private companies. By creating a virtual representation of a system or process, it becomes easier to identify inconsistencies or inefficiencies and develop common standards. This can lead to improved interoperability and smoother integration of IT systems, ultimately enhancing collaboration and efficiency.
3. Simulation and testing: Digital Twins can be used for simulation and testing purposes, allowing member states and private companies to evaluate the interoperability of their IT systems before implementation. By creating virtual replicas, stakeholders can simulate different scenarios, identify potential issues, and make necessary adjustments to ensure seamless interoperability. This can help in reducing risks and costs associated with system integration and deployment.
4. Cross-domain collaboration: Digital Twin technology can facilitate cross-domain collaboration among member states and private companies. By creating a virtual representation of a system or asset, stakeholders from different domains can collaborate and exchange information more effectively. For example, in smart city initiatives, Digital Twins can enable collaboration between transportation, energy, and public safety sectors, leading to improved interoperability and better overall performance.
5. Data-driven decision making: Digital Twins generate vast amounts of data, which can be leveraged for data-driven decision making. By analyzing the data collected from virtual replicas, member states and private companies can gain valuable insights into system performance, identify areas for improvement, and make informed decisions to enhance interoperability. This can lead to optimized operations, improved resource allocation, and better overall outcomes.
Overall, the application of Digital Twin Digital Business Capability can significantly contribute to European IT interoperability among member states and private companies by enabling seamless data sharing, standardization, simulation, cross-domain collaboration, and data-driven decision making.

element.name: Risk analysis
element.documentation:
Description: The 'Risk Analysis' Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of a business to identify, assess, and prioritize potential risks or threats in its digital operations or projects. This capability involves the use of digital tools and technologies to evaluate the likelihood and impact of risks, and to develop strategies to mitigate them. It includes aspects such as cybersecurity risk assessment, data breach risk analysis, and digital project risk management. The aim is to reduce uncertainty, protect business assets, ensure data integrity and privacy, and maintain business continuity in the digital environment.
Additional information: The 'Risk Analysis' Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of an organization to identify, assess, and prioritize risks associated with its digital operations and initiatives. This capability involves the use of digital tools and technologies to evaluate potential threats and vulnerabilities in the organization's digital infrastructure, systems, and processes.
Risk analysis includes the assessment of the potential impact and probability of identified risks, and the development of strategies to manage and mitigate these risks. It involves understanding the organization's risk tolerance and aligning risk management efforts with the organization's strategic objectives and risk appetite.
This capability also includes the ability to monitor and review risks on an ongoing basis, and to adjust risk management strategies as necessary in response to changes in the organization's digital environment or risk profile.
Risk analysis can cover a wide range of risks, including cybersecurity threats, data breaches, technology failures, regulatory compliance risks, and risks associated with digital transformation initiatives.
Effective risk analysis can help an organization to protect its digital assets, ensure the continuity of its digital operations, maintain the trust of its customers and stakeholders, and achieve its strategic objectives in a digital business environment.
In the context of TOGAF, risk analysis is a critical component of the organization's enterprise architecture, helping to ensure that the architecture is robust, resilient, and capable of supporting the organization's business objectives in a risk-informed manner.
Example: 1. Cybersecurity Risk Analysis: Government agencies like the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) or the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in the United States conduct risk analysis to identify potential threats to their digital infrastructure. They assess the likelihood of cyberattacks, their potential impact, and develop strategies to mitigate these risks.
2. Health Risk Analysis: Public health agencies like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) or the World Health Organization (WHO) use digital tools to analyze the risk of disease outbreaks. They use data analytics to predict the spread of diseases, identify high-risk populations, and plan interventions.
3. Financial Risk Analysis: Government financial institutions like the Federal Reserve or the Treasury Department conduct risk analysis to assess the stability of the financial system. They use digital tools to analyze economic indicators, assess the risk of financial crises, and develop strategies to mitigate these risks.
4. Environmental Risk Analysis: Environmental agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) or the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) conduct risk analysis to assess the impact of environmental hazards. They use digital tools to model the impact of climate change, pollution, or natural disasters, and develop strategies to mitigate these risks.
5. Infrastructure Risk Analysis: Public sector entities like the Department of Transportation or the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) conduct risk analysis to assess the resilience of public infrastructure. They use digital tools to model the impact of various hazards, assess the vulnerability of infrastructure, and develop strategies to mitigate these risks.
6. National Security Risk Analysis: Intelligence agencies like the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) or the National Security Agency (NSA) conduct risk analysis to assess threats to national security. They use digital tools to analyze intelligence data, assess the risk of terrorist attacks or other threats, and develop strategies to mitigate these risks.

element.name: Duties Calculation and payment
element.documentation:
Description: 'Duties Calculation and Payment' digital business capability refers to the ability of a business to accurately calculate and process payments related to duties, such as customs duties, taxes, or other levies, using digital tools and platforms. This capability involves the use of advanced software or systems to automate the calculation process, ensure compliance with relevant regulations, and facilitate timely and accurate payments. It may also include features for tracking and reporting duties payments, integrating with other financial systems, and managing duties-related data and documentation. This capability is crucial for businesses involved in international trade or other activities subject to duties.
Additional information: The 'Duties Calculation and Payment' digital business capability refers to the ability of a business to accurately calculate, manage, and process payments related to duties, tariffs, and taxes in a digital environment. This capability is crucial for businesses that operate in international trade, where various types of duties and tariffs apply.
This capability involves several components:
1. Duty Calculation: This involves the use of digital tools and systems to accurately calculate the duties applicable to specific goods or services. This calculation is based on various factors such as the type of goods, their value, their country of origin, and the destination country. The calculation process must comply with the relevant laws and regulations in both the origin and destination countries.
2. Duty Payment Management: Once the duties are calculated, the business must manage the payment process. This involves setting up and maintaining digital payment systems, ensuring secure and timely payment transactions, and managing any issues or disputes that may arise.
3. Compliance and Reporting: The business must also ensure that all duty calculations and payments are compliant with the relevant laws and regulations. This involves maintaining accurate records, generating reports for regulatory bodies, and undergoing audits if required.
4. Integration with Other Systems: The 'Duties Calculation and Payment' capability must be integrated with other business systems, such as supply chain management, finance, and customer relationship management. This ensures that duty calculations and payments are accurately reflected in all relevant business processes and records.
5. Continuous Improvement: The business must continually monitor and improve its 'Duties Calculation and Payment' capability. This involves staying updated with changes in laws and regulations, adopting new technologies and best practices, and addressing any issues or inefficiencies in the process.
In summary, the 'Duties Calculation and Payment' digital business capability is a critical aspect of international trade operations. It requires a combination of accurate calculation, efficient payment management, strict compliance, seamless integration, and continuous improvement.
Example: 1. Customs and Border Protection: In many countries, the customs and border protection department has the responsibility of calculating and collecting duties on imported goods. They use digital systems to assess the value of goods, calculate the applicable duties, and facilitate online payments.
2. Tax Collection Agencies: Tax agencies like the IRS in the United States have digital systems in place for calculating and collecting taxes from individuals and businesses. These systems allow taxpayers to submit their tax returns online, calculate their tax liabilities, and make payments digitally.
3. Social Security Administration: The Social Security Administration in the United States calculates and collects social security taxes from workers' paychecks. They use digital systems to manage these processes.
4. Vehicle Licensing Agencies: In many jurisdictions, vehicle licensing agencies calculate and collect vehicle registration fees, which often include duties or taxes. These agencies often have online systems that allow vehicle owners to pay these fees digitally.
5. Environmental Agencies: Some environmental agencies are responsible for calculating and collecting duties or fees related to environmental regulations. For example, a company might be required to pay a fee based on the amount of pollution it produces. These agencies can use digital systems to manage these processes.
6. Local Government: Local governments often calculate and collect property taxes, utility fees, and other local duties. Many local governments have implemented digital systems that allow residents to pay these fees online.
7. State Liquor Control Boards: In some states, the liquor control board is responsible for calculating and collecting duties on alcohol sales. They may use digital systems to manage these processes.

element.name: Laboratories management
element.documentation:
Description: 'Laboratories Management' as a Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of a business to effectively manage and control its laboratory operations using digital technologies. This includes the use of software and systems for tasks such as scheduling and tracking experiments, managing and analyzing data, maintaining quality control, ensuring regulatory compliance, and managing resources and inventory. It also involves the use of digital tools for communication and collaboration within the laboratory environment. This capability is crucial for improving efficiency, accuracy, and productivity in laboratory operations.
Additional information: The 'Laboratories Management' digital business capability refers to the ability of an organization to effectively manage and control its laboratory operations using digital technologies. This capability encompasses a wide range of activities and processes, including but not limited to, the management of laboratory equipment, materials, and resources, the scheduling and execution of laboratory tests and experiments, the collection, analysis, and reporting of laboratory data, and the compliance with relevant regulations and standards.
In a more detailed perspective, this capability involves the use of digital systems and tools to automate and streamline laboratory processes, improve the accuracy and reliability of laboratory results, enhance the efficiency and productivity of laboratory personnel, and ensure the safety and security of laboratory facilities. It also involves the integration of laboratory systems with other business systems to facilitate the sharing and utilization of laboratory data across the organization.
Moreover, the 'Laboratories Management' digital business capability also includes the ability to leverage advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, and big data analytics to drive innovation and improvement in laboratory operations. This could involve the use of predictive analytics to optimize laboratory workflows, the application of machine learning algorithms to automate complex laboratory tasks, or the use of AI-powered tools to enhance the quality and speed of laboratory decision-making.
Furthermore, this capability also entails the ability to manage the digital transformation of laboratory operations, including the planning, implementation, and management of digital laboratory projects, the training and development of laboratory personnel in the use of digital technologies, and the management of the risks and challenges associated with digital transformation.
In essence, the 'Laboratories Management' digital business capability is about harnessing the power of digital technologies to enhance the performance and value of laboratory operations, and to enable the organization to achieve its strategic objectives in a digital business environment.
Example: 1. National Institute of Health (NIH): The NIH, a part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, is the nation's medical research agency. They use digital capabilities to manage their laboratories, including software for tracking and managing lab equipment, samples, and results, as well as for coordinating research efforts across multiple labs.
2. European Space Agency (ESA): The ESA uses digital capabilities to manage their laboratories, which are involved in a wide range of research and development activities. This includes software for managing lab resources, coordinating research activities, and analyzing and sharing research data.
3. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): The CDC uses digital capabilities to manage their laboratories, which are involved in research and testing related to public health issues. This includes software for managing lab resources, tracking and analyzing test results, and coordinating research efforts.
4. Public Health England (PHE): PHE uses digital capabilities to manage their laboratories, which are involved in research and testing related to public health issues. This includes software for managing lab resources, tracking and analyzing test results, and coordinating research efforts.
5. Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO): ANSTO uses digital capabilities to manage their laboratories, which are involved in nuclear science and technology research. This includes software for managing lab resources, coordinating research activities, and analyzing and sharing research data.
6. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA): NOAA uses digital capabilities to manage their laboratories, which are involved in research related to climate, weather, and ocean conditions. This includes software for managing lab resources, tracking and analyzing research data, and coordinating research efforts.

element.name: Data Lineage
element.documentation:
Description: The Data Lineage Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of an organization to track and trace the origin, movement, and transformation of data throughout its lifecycle. It involves capturing and documenting the lineage of data elements, including their sources, transformations, and destinations. This capability enables organizations to understand the data flow across systems, processes, and applications, ensuring data quality, compliance, and effective decision-making. It also helps in identifying data dependencies, impact analysis, and troubleshooting data-related issues. Overall, the Data Lineage Digital Business Capability provides transparency and visibility into the data ecosystem, facilitating effective data governance and management.
Additional information: The Data Lineage Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of an organization to track and trace the origin, movement, and transformation of data throughout its lifecycle. It involves capturing and documenting the lineage of data elements, including their sources, transformations, and destinations, to ensure data quality, compliance, and understanding.
Data lineage provides a comprehensive view of how data flows through various systems, processes, and applications within an organization. It helps in understanding the data's journey, identifying potential bottlenecks, and ensuring data integrity and accuracy. This capability enables organizations to answer critical questions about data, such as where it comes from, how it is transformed, and where it goes.
The Data Lineage Digital Business Capability encompasses several key components and activities:
1. Data Source Identification: This involves identifying the original sources of data, whether it is internal or external to the organization. It includes understanding the systems, databases, files, or APIs that generate or provide data.
2. Data Transformation Mapping: This component focuses on documenting the transformations applied to data as it moves through different processes, systems, or applications. It includes capturing the rules, algorithms, or logic used to modify or manipulate the data.
3. Data Destination Tracking: This aspect involves tracking the final destinations of data, such as databases, reports, dashboards, or other systems. It ensures that data reaches the intended targets and helps in identifying any potential gaps or inconsistencies.
4. Metadata Management: Metadata, which provides additional context and information about data, plays a crucial role in data lineage. This component involves managing and maintaining metadata repositories, including data dictionaries, data catalogs, and data models.
5. Data Lineage Visualization: Visualizing data lineage helps stakeholders understand the flow of data across systems and processes. It may include graphical representations, diagrams, or interactive tools that depict the relationships and dependencies between data elements.
6. Impact Analysis: Data lineage enables impact analysis by identifying the potential consequences of changes to data sources, transformations, or destinations. It helps in assessing the impact on downstream systems, processes, and reports, facilitating effective change management.
7. Compliance and Audit: Data lineage is essential for regulatory compliance and audit purposes. It enables organizations to demonstrate data lineage to regulatory bodies, ensuring data governance, privacy, and security requirements are met.
8. Data Quality Monitoring: Data lineage supports data quality initiatives by providing insights into the data's journey and identifying potential quality issues. It helps in establishing data quality metrics, monitoring data quality, and implementing corrective actions.
Overall, the Data Lineage Digital Business Capability is a critical aspect of data management and governance. It enables organizations to have a holistic view of their data assets, understand data flows, ensure data integrity, comply with regulations, and make informed decisions based on trustworthy and reliable data.
Example: The Data Lineage Digital Business Capability in the public sector refers to the ability to track and understand the origin, movement, and transformation of data throughout its lifecycle. This capability is crucial for ensuring data quality, compliance, and decision-making. Here are some real examples of how this capability is applied in the public sector:
1. Tax Compliance: In tax administration, data lineage is used to trace the flow of financial data from taxpayers' records to tax returns and subsequent reports. This capability helps auditors and tax authorities verify the accuracy and integrity of the data, ensuring compliance with tax regulations.
2. Fraud Detection: Government agencies responsible for detecting and preventing fraud, such as social welfare fraud or tax evasion, utilize data lineage to track the flow of data across various systems and processes. By analyzing the lineage, anomalies or suspicious patterns can be identified, leading to the detection of fraudulent activities.
3. Public Health Monitoring: Data lineage is crucial in public health monitoring, especially during disease outbreaks or pandemics. It helps track the origin and movement of patient data, test results, and contact tracing information. This capability enables health authorities to identify the source of infection, track the spread of the disease, and make informed decisions for containment and mitigation.
4. Government Performance Reporting: Data lineage is used to ensure the accuracy and reliability of performance reports generated by government agencies. By tracing the data sources, transformations, and calculations involved in generating these reports, data lineage helps maintain transparency, accountability, and trust in the reported performance metrics.
5. Freedom of Information Requests: Public sector organizations often receive requests for information under the Freedom of Information Act or similar legislation. Data lineage helps track the data sources, systems, and processes involved in generating the requested information. This capability ensures that the information provided is accurate, complete, and can be audited if necessary.
These examples demonstrate how the Data Lineage Digital Business Capability is applied in the public sector to ensure data quality, compliance, and informed decision-making.

element.name: Case and Workflow Management
element.documentation:
Definition: Case and Workflow Management enables organisations to design, execute, and automatise internal processes based on pre-defined business rules.
Source: Hajo Reijers
Source reference: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-xg-eiif/2008Oct/att-0019/HARE.MOJA.MIZU.WIAP-BPM-2007.pdf
Additional information: The Case and Workflow Management Digital Business Capability (DWC) is a comprehensive system designed to facilitate and streamline the management of cases and workflows within the context of European IT interoperability among member states and private companies. It serves as a digital platform that enables efficient collaboration, information sharing, and decision-making across various entities involved in the European IT landscape.
The DWC encompasses a range of functionalities and features that support the end-to-end management of cases and workflows. It provides a centralized repository for storing and accessing relevant information, documents, and data related to specific cases or workflows. This ensures that all stakeholders have access to the most up-to-date and accurate information, promoting transparency and accountability.
One of the key aspects of the DWC is its ability to facilitate seamless communication and collaboration among different entities. It enables secure and real-time communication channels, allowing member states and private companies to exchange information, updates, and notifications related to specific cases or workflows. This promotes effective coordination and cooperation, reducing delays and improving overall efficiency.
The DWC also incorporates advanced workflow management capabilities. It allows for the definition and automation of complex workflows, ensuring that tasks and activities are assigned, tracked, and completed in a timely manner. This helps to streamline processes, minimize manual intervention, and reduce the risk of errors or oversights.
Furthermore, the DWC includes robust analytics and reporting functionalities. It enables the generation of comprehensive reports and insights, providing valuable data and metrics related to case and workflow management. This allows member states and private companies to monitor performance, identify bottlenecks, and make data-driven decisions to optimize processes and improve outcomes.
In terms of European IT interoperability, the DWC ensures that member states and private companies can seamlessly integrate their existing IT systems and applications with the platform. It supports standardized data formats, protocols, and interfaces, enabling smooth data exchange and interoperability across different systems. This promotes a cohesive and interconnected IT ecosystem, facilitating efficient collaboration and information sharing among all stakeholders.
Overall, the Case and Workflow Management Digital Business Capability plays a crucial role in enhancing European IT interoperability among member states and private companies. It provides a comprehensive and integrated platform for managing cases and workflows, enabling efficient collaboration, streamlined processes, and improved decision-making. By promoting transparency, accountability, and interoperability, the DWC contributes to the overall effectiveness and efficiency of the European IT landscape.
Example: The following implementation is an example on how this specific Architecture Building Block (ABB) can be instantiated as a Solution Building Block (SBB): ePrescription: "Generation, transmission, and filling of a medical prescription through digital channels. ePrescribing allows a physician, pharmacist, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant to use digital prescription software to electronically transmit a new prescription or renewal authorization to a community or mail-order pharmacy".

element.name: Contact Management
element.documentation:
Definition: Contact Management enables the storing and organisation of contacts of a public administration's user base (both providers and consumers of its public services) and tracking of the related interactions.
Source: Shared Contacts
Source reference: https://www.getsharedcontacts.com/contact-management-guide/
Additional information: The Contact Management Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of European member states and private companies to effectively manage and exchange contact information in a digital format, ensuring interoperability and seamless communication.
In the context of European IT interoperability, member states and private companies need to establish a standardized approach to contact management to facilitate efficient collaboration and information sharing. This capability encompasses various aspects, including the collection, storage, organization, and retrieval of contact information.
At its core, the Contact Management Digital Business Capability involves the adoption of digital tools and technologies to capture and maintain accurate contact details of individuals and organizations. This includes not only basic information such as names, addresses, and phone numbers but also more advanced data like email addresses, social media profiles, and other relevant identifiers.
To ensure interoperability, member states and private companies must adhere to common standards and protocols for contact management. This involves the use of standardized data formats, such as vCard or XML, to enable seamless exchange of contact information across different systems and platforms. Additionally, the capability may involve the implementation of standardized APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) that allow for the integration of contact management systems with other IT systems and applications.
The Contact Management Digital Business Capability also encompasses the implementation of robust security measures to protect the privacy and confidentiality of contact information. This includes encryption techniques, access controls, and data protection policies to prevent unauthorized access, data breaches, or misuse of contact data.
Furthermore, the capability may involve the development and deployment of advanced functionalities to enhance contact management processes. This could include features like deduplication algorithms to identify and eliminate duplicate contacts, integration with CRM (Customer Relationship Management) systems to streamline customer interactions, and automation of contact updates to ensure data accuracy.
In the context of European IT interoperability, the Contact Management Digital Business Capability plays a crucial role in facilitating efficient communication and collaboration among member states and private companies. It enables seamless exchange of contact information, supports effective stakeholder engagement, and enhances overall business processes.
By adopting and implementing this capability, European member states and private companies can establish a standardized and interoperable approach to contact management, leading to improved efficiency, reduced duplication of efforts, and enhanced data quality. This, in turn, contributes to the overall goal of achieving seamless digital integration and collaboration across the European IT landscape.
Example: The Contact Management Digital Business Capability can be applied in various ways to enhance European IT interoperability among member states and private companies. Here are some examples:
1. Centralized Contact Database: A shared contact management system can be established, allowing member states and private companies to maintain a centralized database of contacts. This database can include information about key stakeholders, experts, and decision-makers involved in IT interoperability initiatives. It ensures that up-to-date contact information is readily available to facilitate communication and collaboration.
2. Collaboration Platform: The Contact Management Digital Business Capability can be integrated into a collaboration platform, enabling member states and private companies to connect, share information, and collaborate on IT interoperability projects. This platform can provide features like contact directories, messaging, document sharing, and task management, fostering efficient and effective collaboration across borders.
3. Interoperability Events and Workshops: The capability can be utilized to organize and manage interoperability events and workshops. Member states and private companies can use the contact management system to invite relevant stakeholders, manage registrations, and communicate event details. This ensures that the right people are involved and informed about such events, fostering knowledge exchange and cooperation.
4. Stakeholder Engagement: The Contact Management Digital Business Capability can support member states and private companies in engaging with stakeholders involved in IT interoperability. It can provide tools for identifying and categorizing stakeholders, tracking their interests and concerns, and managing communication with them. This helps in building strong relationships, understanding diverse perspectives, and addressing concerns effectively.
5. Cross-Border Collaboration: The capability can facilitate cross-border collaboration by enabling member states and private companies to identify potential partners and experts in other countries. It can provide a platform for initiating and managing collaboration requests, sharing best practices, and coordinating joint initiatives. This promotes knowledge sharing, innovation, and the development of common standards for IT interoperability.
6. Compliance and Regulatory Management: The Contact Management Digital Business Capability can assist member states and private companies in managing compliance and regulatory requirements related to IT interoperability. It can help track and communicate changes in regulations, maintain contact with regulatory authorities, and ensure timely compliance. This ensures that interoperability initiatives align with legal frameworks and standards across European member states.
Overall, the Contact Management Digital Business Capability plays a crucial role in facilitating communication, collaboration, and stakeholder engagement for IT interoperability among European member states and private companies.

It enables seamless exchange of contact information, supports effective stakeholder engagement, and enhances overall business processes.
By adopting and implementing this capability, European member states and private companies can establish a standardized and interoperable approach to contact management, leading to improved efficiency, reduced duplication of efforts, and enhanced data quality. This, in turn, contributes to the overall goal of achieving seamless digital integration and collaboration across the European IT landscape.

element.name: Expeditions controls
element.documentation:
Description: 'Expeditions controls' digital business capability refers to the ability of a business to effectively manage, monitor, and control its expeditionary activities using digital technologies. This includes planning and coordinating expeditions, tracking the progress and location of expeditions in real-time, ensuring the safety and security of expedition members, managing resources and logistics, and responding to any unexpected incidents or emergencies. This capability may also involve the use of advanced technologies such as GPS tracking, satellite communication, and data analytics to enhance the efficiency, effectiveness, and safety of expedition operations.
Additional information: 'Expeditions Controls' as a Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of a business to effectively manage, monitor, and control all aspects of expeditions or exploratory ventures. This capability is particularly relevant for businesses operating in sectors such as logistics, supply chain, travel, and tourism, or any industry that involves physical movement of goods, people, or resources over long distances.
In the digital context, 'Expeditions Controls' involves the use of advanced technologies and digital solutions to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of expedition management. This could include the use of GPS tracking systems for real-time location monitoring, digital platforms for scheduling and route optimization, IoT devices for condition monitoring (e.g., temperature, humidity, etc.), and AI-powered predictive analytics for risk assessment and mitigation.
Furthermore, 'Expeditions Controls' also encompasses the ability to ensure compliance with relevant regulations and standards, manage potential risks and emergencies, and ensure the safety and well-being of all involved personnel. This could involve digital solutions for documentation and reporting, risk management systems, emergency response systems, and digital training and certification programs.
In essence, 'Expeditions Controls' as a Digital Business Capability is about leveraging digital technologies to enhance the management and control of expeditions, thereby improving operational efficiency, reducing risks, ensuring compliance, and ultimately, enhancing business performance.
Example: 1. National Park Services: The National Park Services in the United States uses digital business capabilities to manage and control expeditions in national parks. They use digital systems to track the number of visitors, manage permits for hiking and camping, and monitor wildlife activity. This helps ensure the safety of visitors and the preservation of natural resources.
2. Disaster Response Teams: Government agencies like FEMA use digital capabilities to control expeditions in disaster-stricken areas. They use digital mapping and tracking systems to coordinate rescue efforts, manage resources, and monitor the progress of relief operations.
3. Space Agencies: Organizations like NASA and the European Space Agency use digital business capabilities to control expeditions in space. They use advanced digital systems to plan missions, monitor spacecraft, and analyze data from space expeditions.
4. Public Health Agencies: Public health agencies use digital capabilities to control expeditions related to disease control and prevention. They use digital systems to track disease outbreaks, manage vaccination campaigns, and monitor public health trends.
5. Archaeological Expeditions: Government bodies responsible for cultural heritage use digital capabilities to control archaeological expeditions. They use digital mapping, 3D modeling, and data analysis tools to plan excavations, document findings, and preserve archaeological sites.
6. Environmental Agencies: Government environmental agencies use digital capabilities to control expeditions related to environmental monitoring and conservation. They use digital systems to track pollution levels, monitor wildlife populations, and manage conservation efforts.
7. Defense and Military Operations: The defense sector uses digital capabilities to control expeditions and operations. They use digital systems for strategic planning, real-time communication, surveillance, and data analysis.

element.name: Artificial Intelligence
element.documentation:
Definition: The capability to connect physical devices, sensors, and objects to the internet, enabling data collection, remote monitoring, and control of devices, and facilitating automation and integration within business processes.
Source: Gartner
Source reference: https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/4008663/hype-cycle-for-artificial-intelligence-2021
Additional information: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Digital Business Capability in the context of European IT interoperability among member states and private companies refers to the integration and utilization of AI technologies to enhance the efficiency, effectiveness, and collaboration in various business processes across Europe.
AI, as a field of computer science, focuses on developing intelligent machines that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence. It encompasses various subfields such as machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and robotics. The application of AI in the digital business realm aims to automate and augment decision-making processes, improve customer experiences, optimize operations, and enable data-driven insights.
In the European Union (EU), IT interoperability refers to the ability of different systems, applications, and devices to seamlessly exchange and use information. It is crucial for member states and private companies to ensure interoperability to facilitate smooth communication, data sharing, and collaboration across borders. The AI Digital Business Capability plays a significant role in achieving this interoperability by leveraging AI technologies to address challenges and unlock opportunities.
One aspect of AI Digital Business Capability is the development and deployment of AI-powered applications and services that can be used by member states and private companies. These applications can range from chatbots and virtual assistants for customer support to predictive analytics tools for business forecasting. By adopting AI-powered solutions, organizations can streamline their operations, improve decision-making processes, and enhance customer experiences.
Furthermore, AI can contribute to the standardization and harmonization of data formats, protocols, and interfaces, which are essential for interoperability. AI algorithms can be employed to analyze and transform data from different sources into a common format, enabling seamless data exchange and integration. This facilitates collaboration and information sharing among member states and private companies, leading to improved efficiency and effectiveness in various domains such as healthcare, transportation, finance, and public administration.
Moreover, AI Digital Business Capability can support the development of AI ecosystems and innovation networks across Europe. By fostering collaboration between member states, research institutions, and private companies, it encourages the exchange of knowledge, expertise, and best practices in AI. This collaboration can lead to the development of AI technologies and solutions that are tailored to the specific needs and challenges of the European context.
To ensure the ethical and responsible use of AI in the European IT interoperability landscape, the EU has also been actively working on establishing guidelines and regulations. The European Commission has proposed the creation of a European AI regulatory framework that promotes transparency, accountability, and human-centric AI. This framework aims to address concerns related to privacy, bias, and fairness in AI systems, ensuring that AI technologies are developed and deployed in a manner that aligns with European values and principles.
In summary, the AI Digital Business Capability in the European IT interoperability context encompasses the integration and utilization of AI technologies to enhance collaboration, efficiency, and effectiveness among member states and private companies. It involves the development of AI-powered applications, the standardization of data formats and interfaces, the fostering of AI ecosystems, and the establishment of ethical guidelines and regulations. By leveraging AI, Europe can unlock the potential of digital transformation, drive innovation, and achieve seamless interoperability in the digital business landscape.
Example: There are several examples of how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can be applied to enhance IT interoperability among member states and private companies in Europe. Here are a few:
1. Data Integration and Standardization: AI can be used to automate the integration and standardization of data across different systems and formats. This helps in achieving seamless interoperability between member states and private companies by ensuring that data can be easily exchanged and understood by all parties involved.
2. Natural Language Processing (NLP): NLP techniques can be employed to enable multilingual communication and understanding between different systems and stakeholders. This facilitates efficient collaboration and information exchange, overcoming language barriers and promoting interoperability.
3. Intelligent Data Mapping: AI algorithms can be utilized to map and align data elements from different systems, enabling interoperability by ensuring that data from various sources can be accurately interpreted and utilized by different entities. This helps in achieving a common understanding of data across member states and private companies.
4. Intelligent Decision Support Systems: AI-powered decision support systems can assist in making complex decisions related to IT interoperability. These systems can analyze vast amounts of data, identify patterns, and provide recommendations for improving interoperability, thereby enhancing efficiency and effectiveness in cross-border collaborations.
5. Predictive Analytics: AI techniques, such as machine learning, can be applied to analyze historical data and predict future trends and patterns. This can help member states and private companies anticipate interoperability challenges and proactively address them, ensuring smooth operations and minimizing disruptions.
6. Intelligent Automation: AI-driven automation can streamline and optimize interoperability processes by automating repetitive tasks, reducing manual effort, and minimizing errors. This can include tasks like data validation, data transformation, and data exchange, enabling efficient and reliable interoperability among different systems.
These are just a few examples of how AI can be applied to enhance IT interoperability among member states and private companies in Europe. The potential applications of AI in this domain are vast and continually evolving as technology advances.

element.name: Electronic Identification
element.documentation:
Definition: Electronic Identification ensures secure access to online services and to carry out electronic transactions in a safer way to citizens or organizations (i.e. public administrations and businesses). Via digital modes, electronic identification can guarantee the unambiguous identification of a person or business and ensures the right service is delivered to the person or business entitled to it. (e.g. government authorities services, digital payments services, ...).
Source reference: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/electronic-identification
Additional information: The Electronic Identification (eID) Digital Business Capability is a crucial component of the European Union's efforts to establish seamless interoperability among member states and private companies in the field of information technology. It aims to provide a standardized and secure framework for electronic identification and authentication across borders, enabling individuals and businesses to access digital services and conduct transactions in a trusted and efficient manner.
At its core, the eID Digital Business Capability revolves around the concept of a digital identity, which serves as a virtual representation of an individual or organization. This digital identity is securely stored and managed by trusted entities, such as government agencies or private service providers, and can be used to establish the identity of the user in various online interactions.
The primary objective of the eID Digital Business Capability is to enable individuals and businesses to use their digital identities to access a wide range of services, both public and private, across different member states. This includes services such as e-government platforms, online banking, e-commerce, healthcare systems, and more. By providing a standardized and interoperable framework, the capability ensures that users can seamlessly authenticate themselves and access these services regardless of their location within the European Union.
To achieve this interoperability, the eID Digital Business Capability relies on a set of technical standards and protocols that enable the secure exchange of identity information between different systems and entities. These standards ensure that digital identities issued by one member state or private entity can be recognized and accepted by others, thereby facilitating cross-border transactions and interactions.
The capability also encompasses the establishment of a network of trust among member states and private entities. This network ensures that the digital identities issued by one entity are trusted and accepted by others, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of the system. This trust network is built upon the principles of mutual recognition, where member states and private entities agree to accept and recognize each other's digital identities based on predefined criteria and standards.
Furthermore, the eID Digital Business Capability places a strong emphasis on privacy and data protection. It ensures that individuals have control over their personal data and can consent to its use for specific purposes. The capability also incorporates mechanisms for secure authentication, such as two-factor authentication or biometric verification, to enhance the overall security of digital transactions.
In summary, the eID Digital Business Capability is a comprehensive framework that aims to establish seamless interoperability among member states and private companies in the European Union. It enables individuals and businesses to use their digital identities to access a wide range of services across borders, while ensuring privacy, security, and trust in the digital ecosystem.
Example: The Electronic Identification (eID) Digital Business Capability has several applications in the context of European IT interoperability among member states and private companies. Here are some examples:
1. Cross-border authentication: eID enables individuals to use their national electronic identification credentials to access online services in other member states. This allows for seamless authentication and access to various services, such as e-government portals, banking, healthcare, and more.
2. Digital signatures and document exchange: eID facilitates the use of digital signatures for secure and legally binding transactions across borders. It enables individuals and businesses to digitally sign documents, contracts, and forms, eliminating the need for physical paperwork and enabling efficient cross-border document exchange.
3. Trusted e-commerce: eID can be used to establish trust in online transactions between businesses and consumers across different member states. It allows for secure identification and authentication of individuals, reducing the risk of fraud and enhancing consumer confidence in cross-border e-commerce.
4. Seamless access to public services: eID enables citizens to access public services in other member states without the need for additional identification procedures. For example, a citizen from one member state can use their eID to access healthcare services or file taxes in another member state, simplifying administrative processes and enhancing cross-border service delivery.
5. Interoperable electronic invoicing: eID can be integrated with electronic invoicing systems to ensure secure and interoperable exchange of invoices between businesses across member states. This streamlines cross-border invoicing processes, reduces administrative burdens, and enhances efficiency in business transactions.
6. Secure data sharing: eID can facilitate secure and controlled sharing of personal data between member states and private companies. It ensures that data is accessed only by authorized individuals or organizations, maintaining privacy and data protection standards while enabling efficient cross-border data exchange for various purposes, such as research, public administration, or business collaborations.
These examples highlight how the application of eID as a digital business capability contributes to European IT interoperability, enabling seamless cross-border transactions, secure data exchange, and efficient access to services across member states and private companies.

element.name: Special procedure
element.documentation:
Description: The 'Special Procedure' digital business capability refers to the ability of a business to execute unique or specialized processes or operations using digital technologies. This could involve the use of advanced software, hardware, or digital tools to carry out tasks that are specific to the business or industry. These special procedures could include proprietary algorithms, unique data analysis methods, specialized manufacturing processes, or any other digital processes that give the business a competitive advantage. This capability is crucial in today's digital age as it allows businesses to differentiate themselves from competitors and deliver unique value to customers.
Additional information: The 'Special Procedure' Digital Business Capability refers to the ability of an organization to execute unique, non-standard processes or operations that are critical to its business model or strategy, leveraging digital technologies. This capability is not about routine, everyday operations but rather about specific procedures that are unique to the organization or its industry.
These special procedures could include anything from complex data analysis, proprietary manufacturing processes, unique service delivery methods, specialized regulatory compliance activities, to innovative customer engagement techniques. They are often the result of an organization's unique expertise, intellectual property, or strategic focus.
The digital aspect of this capability refers to the use of digital technologies to enable, enhance, automate, or transform these special procedures. This could involve the use of advanced analytics, artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics, IoT, blockchain, or other emerging technologies.
The 'Special Procedure' Digital Business Capability requires an organization to have the necessary digital infrastructure, skills, and culture. It also requires a deep understanding of the organization's unique processes and the ability to leverage technology to optimize these processes. This capability can provide a significant competitive advantage, enabling an organization to perform unique procedures more effectively, efficiently, or innovatively than its competitors.
In the context of TOGAF, this capability would be part of the organization's overall enterprise architecture, aligning with its business strategy and objectives, and would need to be carefully managed, governed, and evolved over time.
Example: 1. Online Tax Filing: Many public sector organizations such as the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in the United States have implemented digital business capabilities to allow citizens to file their taxes online. This special procedure involves secure data transmission, automatic calculation of tax obligations, and instant submission of tax forms.
2. Digital Voting: Some countries are experimenting with digital voting systems to increase voter participation and reduce the cost of elections. This involves secure online platforms where citizens can cast their votes, which are then automatically tallied and verified.
3. E-Health Records: Public health organizations are increasingly using digital systems to manage patient records. This involves secure databases where patient information is stored and can be accessed by authorized healthcare professionals.
4. Online License Renewal: Many departments of motor vehicles (DMVs) offer online services for renewing driver's licenses and vehicle registrations. This involves secure online payment systems and automatic updating of DMV records.
5. E-Learning Platforms: Public education institutions are increasingly using digital platforms to deliver courses and educational materials. This involves online learning management systems where students can access course materials, submit assignments, and communicate with teachers.
6. Digital Public Procurement: Governments are implementing digital platforms to manage public procurement processes. This involves online systems where suppliers can submit bids, and public officials can evaluate and award contracts.
7. Online Immigration Services: Immigration departments are offering online services for visa applications and renewals. This involves secure online forms and payment systems, as well as digital systems for tracking application status.
8. E-Government Portals: Many governments have implemented comprehensive e-government portals that provide a wide range of public services online. These portals often involve complex digital systems that integrate various government departments and services.
